proposed_edges.relationship: In “Worrying about Emotions in History” (2002), Rosenwein challenges Peter and Carol Stearns’s restriction of emotionology to sources and assumptions that marginalize the premodern past.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Fresh OCR reading of the allowed Trieste teaching PDF, printed pp. 824–826: “very shallow past” (824) introduces objections to middle-class advice manuals, excluded courtly literature and premodern childishness. Repairs the held proposal’s unread-page gap. Joint credit to Carol Z. Stearns retained; their originals and Peter’s 1992 review remain unread.

review.reviewer: Claude (independent verification agent; coordinator decisions by Claude)
review.phrase_seen: But it turned out to be a very shallow past... emotionology by definition belongs to the modern period
review.reason: OCR of printed pp. 824-826 (university teaching copy of the single article, allowed). Rosenwein objects to middle-class advice manuals as the only emotionology source, the exclusion of courtly love literature (p. 825), and the Stearnses' 'childlike' premodern picture; p. 826 'This is a very narrow time frame.' Joint Peter and Carol Stearns target correctly noted; June 2002 date correct. No existing duplicate edge.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Worrying about Emotions in History” (2002), Rosenwein questions Delumeau’s inference of experienced fear from frightening representations, while praising his range of sources.
proposed_edges.map_label: Questions inference from images to fear
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Fresh teaching-copy OCR, printed pp. 832–833, especially 833: “from scary sources to real fear?” addresses Delumeau and Peter Dinzelbacher together. Delumeau’s church-centred account is distinguished from Elias’s state-centred account. Sin and Fear and Dinzelbacher’s book remain unread; this is Rosenwein’s objection.

review.reviewer: Claude (independent verification agent; coordinator decisions by Claude)
review.phrase_seen: marvelous breadth of sources... But are they right to jump from scary sources to real fear?
review.reason: Printed p. 833 (OCR) matches exactly: praise of breadth of sources, then the question about inferring real fear; p. 832-833 also places Delumeau's church-as-'civilizer' account within the grand narrative. Sentence is bounded and accurate.

proposed_edges.relationship: Rosenwein coordinated the exchange with Patrick Geary, Richard Landes, Amy G. Remensnyder and Timothy Reuter published as “Qui a peur de l’an mil ?” (1999), following their 1998 email discussion.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Fresh primary opening page, Médiévales 37 (1999), p. 15, read through Persée: byline gives Rosenwein “coordination”; introductory paragraph names the four participants, dates the emails 15 January–15 February 1998, and credits her “mise en scène et la mise en forme”. Her opening questions about the millennium were read. This is an undirected editorial collaboration, not sole co-authorship or agreement about the year 1000. Bernadette Grandcolas is credited as translator. Discussion pp. 16–55 and the unabridged emails remain unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: Alain Guerreau’s 1990 review identifies Mauss’s Essai sur le don as a central resource for Rosenwein’s interpretation of Cluny’s property transfers in To Be the Neighbor of Saint Peter (1989).
proposed_edges.map_label: Gift theory into Cluny property study
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Mediated evidence: Guerreau’s own review, printed p. 97, final paragraph, freshly read in Persée’s page-specific text. He names Mauss’s essay as “Le texte capital” for the anthropology of gifts through which she interprets property transfers; Malinowski, Finley, Grierson and Duby also appear as resources. This verifies the reviewer’s attribution, not Rosenwein’s own wording or an endorsement by Guerreau. The book and Mauss’s essay were not read. Page 98 could not be fetched; the rest of the review remains unread. Original 1989 book date is independently listed in the freshly checked Loyola bibliography.
